newsitem.title: MACEDONIA: Macedonia holds high-stakes local election.
newsitem.headline: Macedonia holds high-stakes local election.

text.p: Macedonians began voting on Sunday in local elections that political analysts said would decide whether the country sticks to sweeping free-market reforms adopted by the ruling party.
Polls opened at 7 a.m. and were due to close at 7 p.m. as voters chose municipal councils and mayors in an election that was being treated as a referendum on the current national government.
It was the first local ballot under the country's new council system established after Macedonia split away from the former Yugoslav Federation in 1991.

The election pits the ruling Social Democrats, who have pursued rapid economic reform, against opposition parties which have urged a slower approach and described the government's privatisation programme as "unjust".
"The prime minister (Branko Crvenkovski) will have to face the truth of these elections," opposition parliament member Naum Simjanovski told Reuters.
"These elections will legalise the political alternatives that Crvenkovski has ignored until now. They will show how out of touch he is with the people and with alternative views."
Simjanovski said rival parties saw the vote as a crucial test of their electoral appeal.
"The results will be analysed to give us clues about how we should run parliamentary elections in 1998 and the presidential election the following year," the Liberal Party member said.
The two sides also differ over Greece, where a dispute over Macedonia's name has damaged relations between Athens and Skopje.
The Social Democrats have taken a pragmatic approach and argued for compromise with Greece, while the opposition VMRO-DPMNE says Macedonia must fight harder to protect its national identity.
Diplomats say a large ethnic Albanian minority in western districts may be the most volatile factor in Macedonia's political scene.
Ethnic Albanian leaders have accused the Macedonian government of denying Albanians equal rights in education and have demanded permission to open their own university in the town of Tetovo.
Big gains by Albanian parties could increase ethnic tensions in the former Yugoslav republic, which borders the predominantly Albanian province of Kosovo in neighbouring Serbia.
First unofficial results are expected by late on Monday, election officials said.
One Western diplomat said new electoral rules would make it difficult to interpret the results of the vote.

Under the old Yugoslavia, Macedonia had 34 local council districts, whereas now there are 124. There are also over 14,000 candidates -- one per cent of the population -- competing for the council jobs.

"The fact is that the electorate has never been tested like this before. How can you judge what they think about national issues when the local council system is so fragmented and when you have no previous results to compare it with?" said the diplomat.
But the ruling Social Democrats seemed to have no doubts about what Macedonians were voting for.

As voters walked to polling stations, they passed along streets plastered with Social Democrat campaign posters -- most bearing photos not of local candidates, but of Prime Minister Crvenkovski surrounded by his grinning cabinet.
